tags.name: payments
tags.description: Provider callbacks. The authoritative signal that money moved.

tags.name: operations
tags.description: The work the machine could not finish on its own: dead-lettered notifications, and the queue somebody is looking at. Platform-scoped, redacted, and audited — an operations tool is read on shared screens, so it shows statuses rather than customers’ mail.

tags.name: webhooks
tags.description: Provider callbacks. The authoritative signal that money moved, verified over the exact bytes sent.

tags.name: analytics
tags.description: What an organiser’s events actually did: tickets gone, seats left, people admitted, refunds and disputes outstanding, and the money behind all of it. Every figure is counted from the record it belongs to — money from the append-only ledger, inventory from the seats themselves — and a measurement this system does not record is named as missing rather than estimated.

tags.name: finance
tags.description: Money leaving: what an organiser is owed, what is held against it, and the payouts, transfers and disputes that move it. Every figure is derived from the append-only ledger rather than read off a column, and a reversal posts compensating entries rather than editing history.

tags.name: refunds
tags.description: Giving money back: requesting, approving, submitting and withdrawing. Every amount is computed from the order, every step is audited, and the provider is called with no transaction open — a refund is the one commerce action where every failure mode costs somebody money.

tags.name: tickets
tags.description: Door scanning and attendance.

tags.name: traffic
tags.description: Counting visits to event pages without cookies or stored addresses, and the platform view of every event’s visits.

tags.name: media
tags.description: Pictures organisers upload, served only once a moderator has approved them and the event is public; bytes are rebuilt from the image data and stripped of metadata before they are stored.

tags.name: waitlist
tags.description: Waitlist sign-up for sold-out events.

tags.name: imports
tags.description: Bringing events listed on another site onto Desi-Event, by the Desi-Event team.

tags.name: referral-codes
tags.description: Codes the Desi-Event team hands out that remove the booking fee from an order. Made, changed and reported by platform administrators.

tags.name: platform
tags.description: Platform staff administration: accounts, platform roles, direct organisation membership, and organiser invitations.

tags.name: privacy
tags.description: Redacting a person’s personal data, and the record of having done it. Organisation-scoped and never platform-wide: one request names one subject inside one organisation. Redaction is irreversible — no reversal path, original value, encrypted copy or recoverable mapping is stored — so every command here needs the narrow `privacy:redact` capability, a step-up no older than two minutes, and a single-use confirmation the server issued. Nothing on this surface returns a value that was or will be redacted: a request is described by counts and categories, and the subject by an opaque id.

post.description: Exchange email and password for a session, returned both as a cookie and as a bearer token carrying the same secret. A wrong password and an unknown email answer identically, and both pay the same hashing cost, so neither the body nor the response time enumerates accounts. An account with a second factor and no code supplied answers 200 with `mfaRequired` rather than an error — an error would have to distinguish "wrong password" from "right password, now show a code", which tells an attacker which passwords are correct. Failures are counted per address and per source, and a caller past either threshold gets 429 with no indication of which counter tripped.

get.summary: List the team
get.description:
Everybody in this organisation, the invitations still outstanding, and the roles the caller may grant. The role list is computed from what the caller holds rather than fixed, because a member cannot grant a power they do not have. Carries each person's name and nothing else about their account. Addresses are decided by the server and carried in one of three shapes told apart by `emailVisibility`. `FULL` needs `team:role_manage` held through the caller's own membership of this organisation (ADMIN, OWNER) and a second factor confirmed within the `MEMBER_EMAIL_VIEW` step-up window. `STEP_UP_REQUIRED` is the same caller without that recent confirmation: no addresses, and a step-up followed by a second request will show them. `HIDDEN` is everybody else who may read the list (MANAGER, EVENT_MANAGER, FINANCE, STAFF, VIEWER, and a platform super administrator who is not a member): no address field at all, and names carrying an address have it replaced with `Hidden email`. SCANNER cannot read the list. `assignableRoles` lists only roles that neither create nor publish events (FINANCE, STAFF, SCANNER, VIEWER, bounded by what the caller holds): roles that post events are given by the Desi-Event team. Each member carries `postsEvents`, and `roleChoices`, the roles this caller may move that member to — empty for the caller and for an owner, and a posting role only downwards for somebody who already posts.

Requires the `organization:view_members` capability.

post.description:
Issue a single-use invitation code for an email address, for a role bounded by what the caller holds: a member cannot invite somebody to a role that carries powers they lack, and OWNER cannot be invited at all. Roles that create or publish events (event manager, manager, administrator) are given by the Desi-Event team, and inviting somebody to one answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM` with nothing written. An address that already belongs to the organisation answers 409. A second invitation to the same address supersedes the first, and the database holds at most one live invitation per address, so two issued at the same moment produce one invitation and one 409. How the code reaches the invitee is the deployment’s `DELIVERY_MODE`. In `MANUAL`, the default, `data.delivery.invitationCode` carries the code, returned exactly once, in this 201 only, with `cache-control: no-store, private`; it is never logged or audited, and only its SHA-256 digest is stored, so nobody can show it again. The inviter hands it over themselves. In `EMAIL` (`DELIVERY_MODE=EMAIL` with an SMTP server configured) the mail server sends it, `invitationCode` is null, and an address that has already been sent three codes from Desi-Event in the last day answers 429 `RECIPIENT_DAILY_LIMIT`; if the server refuses the message, the invitation is withdrawn and the answer is 503 `DELIVERY_FAILED`, so no code is left live that nobody holds. Waits behind other changes to the organisation or to the address for a bounded time (503 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` with `Retry-After`, nothing issued and nothing sent).

Requires the `team:invite` capability.

post.description: Join an organisation with an invitation code, typed rather than followed from a link. The caller must be signed in as the address the invitation names — a code passed on to somebody else does not work for them, which is what stops an invitation becoming a transferable key, and the refusal names no part of that address. Single-use, enforced by a conditional update, so two simultaneous acceptances produce one membership. Joining is a privilege change (finding NF-10): every other session the caller holds ends, a cookie session is given a new secret, and the session is shortened to the privileged lifetime when the new role is privileged. `data.joined` is false when the account already belonged to the organisation: the code is spent, the existing role is unchanged and no session ends. `data.session` says whether the account now needs a second factor and whether it has one. A direct grant that adds the account at the same moment answers 409 and leaves the code usable. An invitation that offers a role which creates or publishes events (one written before such invitations were withdrawn) answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM` and is not spent, and an organiser invitation code answers 403 `WRONG_INVITATION_KIND` and is not spent either. Rate limited per account.

post.summary: Issue a new code for an invitation
post.description:
For a code that was lost, never handed over, or issued before codes were shown to the inviter. The outstanding invitation is withdrawn and a new one is issued for the same address and role in one transaction, so the old code stops working at the moment the new one exists. Bounded like an invitation: the caller must be able to grant the invitation’s role, so a MANAGER cannot obtain a code for a FINANCE invitation an owner issued. Keyed by the invitation, because a caller who may not see addresses cannot retype one. The new code is returned exactly as `teams.invite` returns one: once, with `cache-control: no-store, private`, never logged or audited; in `EMAIL` it is sent, with the same daily limit per address and the same withdrawal and 503 `DELIVERY_FAILED` when the mail server refuses it. An invitation offering a role that creates or publishes events answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM`. An invitation that is no longer outstanding answers 409, and one belonging to another organisation 404. Waits behind other changes to the organisation or to the address for a bounded time (503 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` with `Retry-After`, no new code issued and the old one still working).

Requires the `team:invite` capability.

post.description:
The only way an owner stops being one and somebody else starts, done as one swap: the named member becomes OWNER and the caller becomes ADMIN, in one transaction with the owners locked, so there is never a moment with no owner or a second one nobody meant. Only an OWNER of this organisation may do it, through their own membership — a platform super administrator uses the audited direct grant instead. Requires a second factor confirmed within the SECURITY_ROLE window. The new owner’s sessions all end, so they sign in again under the role they now hold; the caller’s cookie session is given a new secret. The caller cannot name themselves (403), and a membership of another organisation, or one removed while the transfer waited, is not found (404) and nothing changes. The heir must already create events here — an event manager, manager or administrator — or the answer is 422 `HEIR_MUST_POST_EVENTS`, so a transfer never makes somebody new a poster of events.

Requires the `organization:manage` capability.

patch.description:
Bounded three ways. The caller must be able to grant the new role and must already hold power over the old one, so nobody can promote somebody past themselves or demote somebody above them. Nobody may change their own role, which is what stops a MANAGER making themselves an ADMIN. And the last OWNER cannot be demoted: an organisation with no owner is one nobody can fix. Each of these is decided from the member’s role as it stands once their row and the owners’ are locked, so an ownership transfer landing at the same moment cannot turn a permitted change into the demotion of an owner. A role that creates or publishes events is set only on a member who already holds one, and only downwards (to a role whose powers are a subset of theirs); any other move to such a role answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM`, because who posts events is decided by the Desi-Event team.

Requires the `team:role_manage` capability.

post.description:
Any of the seven platform roles — ATTENDEE, ORGANIZER, SUPPORT, MODERATOR, FINANCE_ADMIN, ADMIN (the platform administrator, who invites organisers and reviews) and SUPER_ADMIN — with a written reason recorded on the audit row. Super administrators (`platform:admin`) only, with a second factor confirmed within the SECURITY_ROLE window. Never the caller’s own account (403). get.description:
Money, inventory, attendance and operations for one organisation, in one call. The monetary figures are the finance view’s — derived from the append-only ledger, never from order totals — and everything else is counted from the rows that are the fact: `Ticket`, `EventSeat`, `CheckIn`. The two are separate branches of the payload on purpose, because "tickets sold × face value" is not revenue and a screen that prints it beside a ledger figure invites somebody to reconcile two different measurements. Every window and date bucket is UTC and the payload says so. `organizationId` is required: this view is always one organisation’s (the platform-wide list of events is `traffic.events`, held by `analytics:view_all`), and an optional organisation is how an organisation capability quietly becomes a platform one. Requires `report:view` in that organisation. The monetary branch additionally requires `finance:view` **and** a second factor confirmed within the `FINANCE_VIEW` window; without either it is absent from the payload rather than hidden by the screen, and `moneyWithheld` says which of the two was missing. The counts are not withheld for a stale session, because a door steward reading an attendance figure is not a financial action. `traffic` counts visits to the organisation’s public event pages in whole UTC days: page views, visitors (distinct per event per day), event-card clicks and where they happened, ‘Choose tickets’ and ‘Choose seats’ presses, visits sent to the organiser’s website, where page views came from as five categories, a per-day series (at most 366 days), and paid orders against visitors. It is read from daily totals that a background job brings up to date (every ten minutes by default); `traffic.updatedAt` says when it last did, and `traffic.stale` is set when that is over two hours ago. Robots, signed-in members of the organisation and Desi-Event staff are not counted; a browser sending Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track is counted in views, never in visitors. Deleted events are listed, marked `deleted`. `eventId` narrows it to one event, and an event of another organisation matches nothing. `funnel.atVenue.bookedUnpaid` counts orders booked to pay at the venue that are still waiting for a payment at the door, which are not counted as paid; `venuePayments` gives the tickets still unpaid at the door, what they owe, what was taken at the door — by the organiser, so outside the money figures, which come from the ledger — and how many unpaid tickets were cancelled (`cancelledUnpaidTickets`). A ticket cancelled unpaid gave its place back, so sold counts leave it out and each breakdown group says how many there were (`cancelledQuantity`).

Requires the `report:view` capability.

When the charge succeeds but the order cannot be completed, the capture is recorded for reconciliation and the answer is a 500 `ORDER_NOT_COMPLETED`; a capture the provider did not answer is a 502 `PAYMENT_TIMEOUT`. Both leave the order PENDING, name it in `error.orderReference`, and tell the buyer not to pay again, in production too. post.description: Resolves a scanned pass or a printed code and says what a door needs to decide: the event and its time, the tier, the seat, the attendee's name, whether the ticket is already in, and a closed refusal reason when it may not be admitted. post.description: Creates an invitation and returns it. The ticket does not move: TRANSFER_PENDING means somebody has been asked, and the current holder can still be admitted — an invitation nobody accepted must not leave a paying attendee at the door. Either way the recipient must be signed in at the offered address to use it, and the code is never logged, audited or put in the notification outbox. In `EMAIL` two limits keep this from becoming a way to email strangers: a sender may email five transfer codes an hour (429), and an address that has already been sent three codes from Desi-Event in the last day answers 429 `RECIPIENT_DAILY_LIMIT`; if the mail server refuses the message, the offer is withdrawn, the ticket is the holder’s again, and the answer is 503 `DELIVERY_FAILED`.

post.description:
An organiser saying this particular ticket no longer admits anybody. Distinct from a refund, which is about money, and from a cancellation, which is about the event — revoking does not give anything back, and a reason is required because nothing else will say why somebody was turned away. The pass dies with it. When the order then has no ticket left and nothing left to refund, its referral use is given back. Waits behind other changes to the ticket’s order for a bounded time (503 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` with `Retry-After`, the ticket still valid). Requires `ticket:revoke`.

Requires a recent step-up authentication: see `POST /v1/auth/step-up`.

sessionCookie.description: The session cookie set by `POST /v1/auth/login`. A state-changing request must also echo the `__Host-desi_csrf` cookie in the `x-desi-csrf` header and arrive from an expected origin. On a deployment served over plain HTTP the cookies lose their `__Host-` prefix.

bearerAuth.description: The same session secret `POST /v1/auth/login` returns as `token`, presented as a bearer token instead of a cookie. Opaque, not a JWT: it is the key to a session row, so revoking the session revokes the token.
